pos: n. (a person of unusually small stature; among the blemishes barring a priest from the altar)
etymology: Old English dweorg, a person of small stature. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the list of bodily blemishes that disqualified a son of Aaron from offering, where the Hebrew word suggests one who is slight or wasted.
biblical_def: Or crookbackt, or a dwarf, or that hath a blemish in his eye, or be scurvy, or scabbed. The list is part of the law of the priesthood, and it must be read with the two verses that follow it or it will be badly misread. No man that hath a blemish of the seed of Aaron the priest shall come nigh to offer the offerings of the LORD made by fire. But then: He shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy. Only he shall not go in unto the vail, nor come nigh unto the altar. The man remains a priest, remains of the seed of Aaron, remains fed from the holy things at the same table as his brethren; what he may not do is stand at the altar. The reason given is not about his worth but about the sign: that he profane not my sanctuaries; for I the LORD do sanctify them. Every detail of the Levitical system was a picture of an unblemished priest offering an unblemished sacrifice, and a marred body in that office would have blurred the picture. Hebrews names the One the picture was for: such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a general name for an animal or plant which is much below the ordinary size of the species; in Scripture, one of the blemishes barring a son of Aaron from the altar.
webster_full: DWARF, n. A general name for an animal or plant which is much below the ordinary size of the species.
BLEMISH, n. Any mark of deformity; any scar or defect that diminishes beauty or renders imperfect.
PRIEST, n. A man who officiates in sacred offices; among Christians, a person who officiates at the altar.
TYPE, n. A sign; a symbol; a figure of something to come.
UNBLEMISHED, a. Free from turpitude or reproach; free from spot or defect.
scriptures: No man that hath a blemish of the seed of Aaron the priest shall come nigh to offer the offerings of the LORD made by fire: he hath a blemish; he shall not come nigh to offer the bread of his God.
He shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy.
Only he shall not go in unto the vail, nor come nigh unto the altar, because he hath a blemish; that he profane not my sanctuaries: for I the LORD do sanctify them.
Heb 7:26
For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens;
corruption_summary: The blemish laws are read as contempt for the disabled, when the text keeps the blemished priest in the priesthood and at the holy table and bars him only from the altar, for the sake of the type it was picturing.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge that Leviticus 21 despises the disabled collapses on verse 22. He shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy. He is not demoted, excluded from the sanctuary, or cut off from the covenant; he eats the priestly portion with his brothers. What he may not do is perform the one act that functioned as a picture — an unblemished man bringing an unblemished offering. The same chapter requires the animals to be without blemish for the identical reason. The law is protecting a sign, not ranking men, and the sign was for Christ.

It matters that the Lord's own ministry ran in the opposite direction on the human level. He touched lepers, healed the blind and the lame in the temple courts, and told a host to invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind, for they cannot recompense thee. The image of God in every person is affirmed whole, whatever the body does or fails to do; and in the resurrection the body itself is raised in glory. The altar was closed for a season to guard a shadow, and the substance came and opened the way for everyone.
roots_summary: Hebrew daq (H1851), thin, small, slight; muwm (H3971), a blemish or spot; qarab (H7126), to come near or approach.
roots_lines: Hebrew daq (H1851) — thin, slight, small; rendered dwarf at Leviticus 21:20.
Hebrew muwm (H3971) — a blemish, a spot, a defect; he hath a blemish.
Hebrew qarab (H7126) — to draw near, to approach, to offer; he shall not come nigh to offer.
Hebrew lechem (H3899) — bread, food; he shall eat the bread of his God.
Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to sanctify, to set apart; I the LORD do sanctify them.
usage: “or a dwarf, or that hath a blemish in his eye” — the single occurrence.
“He shall eat the bread of his God” — the verse that governs the reading.
“such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled” — what the type was for.

pos: n. (in bloody flux, dysentery; the illness of the father of Publius)
etymology: From Latin fluxus, a flowing. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the phrase bloody flux, of the sickness Paul found on Melita after the shipwreck.
biblical_def: And it came to pass, that the father of Publius lay sick of a fever and of a bloody flux: to whom Paul entered in, and prayed, and laid his hands on him, and healed him. Luke is a physician and names the complaint precisely. The setting is worth noticing: Paul has just come ashore from a wreck, has been bitten by a viper while gathering sticks for the fire, and has been watched by the islanders who first decided he was a murderer whom vengeance suffereth not to live and then, when he shook the beast off and felt no harm, changed their minds and said that he was a god. Between those two false verdicts, the apostle is quietly doing the ordinary work: gathering firewood, praying for a sick old man, healing him. And once this was done, others also which had diseases in the island came, and were healed. It is one of the clearest pictures in Acts of a servant who is neither destroyed by the crowd's hostility nor flattered by its worship, and the barbarous people who had shewed the castaways no little kindness received far more than they gave.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of flowing; also, a disease called dysentery, in which the discharges are mixed with blood.
webster_full: FLUX, n. The act of flowing; the motion or passing of a fluid.
FLUX, n. A disease of the bowels; dysentery; the bloody flux.
FEVER, n. A disease characterized by an accelerated pulse, with increase of heat and disturbed functions.
BARBAROUS, a. In a general sense, foreign; in the Greek usage, one who did not speak Greek.
HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers without reward.
scriptures: Act 28:8
And it came to pass, that the father of Publius lay sick of a fever and of a bloody flux: to whom Paul entered in, and prayed, and laid his hands on him, and healed him.
Act 28:2
And the barbarous people shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one, because of the present rain, and because of the cold.
Act 28:6

Howbeit they looked when he should have swollen, or fallen down dead suddenly: but after they had looked a great while, and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.
Act 28:9
So when this was done, others also, which had diseases in the island, came, and were healed:
corruption_summary: A minister is weighed by the crowd's verdict, which swings between condemnation and adulation within a single afternoon on Melita; Paul accepted neither and kept to the work in front of him.
corruption_paragraphs: The islanders' two judgments about Paul are separated by a few minutes and both are wrong. First, no doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live — a confident reading of providence off a snakebite. Then, when nothing happened, they said that he was a god. The same crowd had made the same reversal at Lystra in the other order, calling Paul Mercurius and preparing oxen for sacrifice, and then stoning him and dragging him out of the city supposing he had been dead. A ministry built on public estimate is built on that.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself, and the principle to recover is the servant's indifference to the verdict of the crowd. Paul's own rule was written to a church that was assessing him: with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man's judgment; he that judgeth me is the Lord. The work on Melita was firewood, prayer, and laid-on hands, done for a sick man in a house, and the island was healed around it.
roots_summary: Greek dusenteria (G1420), dysentery, the bloody flux; puretos (G4446), a fever; iaomai (G2390), to heal or cure.
roots_lines: Greek dusenteria (G1420) — dysentery, the bloody flux; the one occurrence, Acts 28:8.
Greek puretos (G4446) — a fever, a burning heat; sick of a fever.
Greek iaomai (G2390) — to heal, to cure; and healed him.
Greek therapeuo (G2323) — to serve, to tend, to heal; came, and were healed.
Greek philanthropia (G5363) — kindness toward men; shewed us no little kindness.
usage: “sick of a fever and of a bloody flux” — the single occurrence, named by a physician.
“said that he was a god” — the crowd's second verdict in an afternoon.
“others also, which had diseases in the island, came, and were healed” — what followed.

pos: n. (the stomach of a beast; part of the priest's due from every sacrifice)
etymology: Old English maga, the stomach. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the law of the priests' portion, naming the shoulder, the two cheeks, and the maw as what the offerer owed to the priest.
biblical_def: And this shall be the priest's due from the people, from them that offer a sacrifice, whether it be ox or sheep; and they shall give unto the priest the shoulder, and the two cheeks, and the maw. Three specific parts, named so that neither the offerer nor the priest would have to negotiate. The context is the law of the ministry in Deuteronomy 18: the priests the Levites, and all the tribe of Levi, shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel; they shall eat the offerings of the LORD made by fire, and his inheritance. A tribe with no land was to be supported by the worship of the nation, and the support was specified down to the cut of meat. This is the Old Testament foundation of one of Paul's plainest apostolic rulings: do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar? Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel. The homeliest of words, a beast's stomach, stands at the head of the Bible's doctrine of ministerial support.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the stomach of brutes; in Scripture, one of the three parts of every sacrifice due to the priest.
webster_full: MAW, n. The stomach of brutes; applied to the stomach of man in contempt.
DUE, n. That which is owed; that which one contracts to pay, do or perform to another.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession.
MAINTENANCE, n. Sustenance; sustentation; support by means of supplies.
scriptures: Deu 18:3
And this shall be the priest's due from the people, from them that offer a sacrifice, whether it be ox or sheep; and they shall give unto the priest the shoulder, and the two cheeks, and the maw.
Deu 18:1
The priests the Levites, and all the tribe of Levi, shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel: they shall eat the offerings of the LORD made by fire, and his inheritance.
Do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar?
Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
corruption_summary: Ministerial support is treated either as an embarrassment to be apologised for or as a market in which a preacher sets his own rate; Scripture makes it a due, specified by God, owed by the people and not negotiated by the minister.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 18 removes the two errors at once by making the support a matter of law rather than of generosity or of leverage. The Levite had no land by God's own arrangement, so his provision was structural, and the parts were named so no one could shave the portion. Paul argues the same way in 1 Corinthians 9, from the ox treading out the corn and from the altar, and then — having established the right at length — declines to use it at Corinth, so that he might make the gospel of Christ without charge. The right is real, and a man may waive his own right.

What Scripture will not tolerate is the corruption of the portion into an appetite, which is exactly what the sons of Eli did with the fleshhook a few centuries after this law was given, and what Micah of Ephraim purchased with ten shekels a year. Peter's charge to elders keeps both sides: feed the flock of God, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind. The maw is owed; the man who serves for the maw has already lost the office.
roots_summary: Hebrew qebah (H6896), the stomach or maw; mishpat (H4941), a due or right; zeroa' (H2220), the shoulder or arm.
roots_lines: Hebrew qebah (H6896) — the stomach or maw of a beast; the one occurrence, Deuteronomy 18:3.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — a judgment, a right, a due; the priest's due from the people.

“shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel” — why the due was needed.
“they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” — the apostolic ruling.

pos: n. (the spine; the line along which the fat of the peace offering was taken off)
etymology: From back and bone. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the law of the peace offering, where the whole rump was to be taken off hard by the backbone.
biblical_def: And he shall offer of the sacrifice of the peace offering an offering made by fire unto the LORD; the fat thereof, and the whole rump, it shall he take off hard by the backbone. The instruction is anatomical because the offering was exact. The peace offering was the one sacrifice the worshipper ate from, a meal shared before God, and yet the choicest portion — the fat — was burned and never eaten by anyone. Leviticus states the rule in plain words at the end of the chapter: it shall be a perpetual statute for your generations throughout all your dwellings, that ye eat neither fat nor blood; all the fat is the LORD's. The reservation is the doctrine. In a meal of fellowship, the best is God's by right and is put beyond every human appetite. The blood is withheld for a different reason, given in Leviticus 17: the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls. And the smoke of the burning is called a sweet savour unto the LORD, a phrase Paul takes up for Christ, who gave himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the spine or vertebral column of an animal; in Scripture, the line along which the fat of the peace offering was severed.
webster_full: BACKBONE, n. The bone of the back; the spine; the vertebral column.
RUMP, n. The end of the backbone of an animal, with the parts adjacent.
PEACE-OFFERING, n. Among the Jews, an offering or sacrifice made to God to procure peace and reconciliation.
FAT, n. In Scripture, the richest or choicest part, reserved to the LORD upon the altar.
ATONEMENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury.
scriptures: Lev 3:9

And he shall offer of the sacrifice of the peace offering an offering made by fire unto the LORD; the fat thereof, and the whole rump, it shall he take off hard by the backbone; and the fat that covereth the inwards, and all the fat that is upon the inwards,
Lev 3:16
And the priest shall burn them upon the altar: it is the food of the offering made by fire for a sweet savour: all the fat is the LORD'S.
Lev 3:5
And Aaron's sons shall burn it on the altar upon the burnt sacrifice, which is upon the wood that is on the fire: it is an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD.
For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.
corruption_summary: Worship is arranged around what the worshipper gets from it, so that God receives the remainder; the peace offering gave the worshipper a meal and reserved the choicest part entirely for God.
corruption_paragraphs: The peace offering is the friendliest of the sacrifices — a shared meal, eaten in God's presence, an occasion of joy — which is precisely what makes its reservation so pointed. All the fat is the LORD's. The richest portion of the animal, the part any diner would want, is burned where no one can have it, every time, as a perpetual statute. A worship in which God gets what is left after the congregation's preferences have been served has inverted the offering, however warm the fellowship feels.

Malachi is the prophet of that inversion, and his charge is that the priests offered the blind, the lame, and the sick for sacrifice and then said the table of the LORD was contemptible. Offer it now unto thy governor, he says; will he be pleased with thee? The dictionary holds the regulative principle for the same reason Leviticus specifies the cut of fat: God, not the worshipper, determines what is acceptable in his worship. And the law of the blood points past all of it to the one sacrifice that made peace, for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.

pos: n. pl. (the hair above the eyes; shaved in the cleansing of the leper)
etymology: From eye and brow, Old English bru. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in the ritual of the seventh day of the leper's cleansing, where all his hair is shaved off, the eyebrows named among the rest.
biblical_def: But it shall be on the seventh day, that he shall shave all his hair off his head and his beard and his eyebrows, even all his hair he shall shave off: and he shall wash his clothes, also he shall wash his flesh in water, and he shall be clean. The naming of the eyebrows is the thoroughness of the law made visible. Nothing is left. The whole ritual in Leviticus 14 is elaborate — two birds, one killed over running water in an earthen vessel and one dipped in its blood and let loose into the open field, cedar wood, scarlet, hyssop, sprinkling seven times, washing, shaving, a second shaving seven days later, then offerings and blood and oil put on the tip of the right ear and the thumb of the right hand and the great toe of the right foot. It is the most detailed cleansing in the law, and it could not be begun until the leprosy was already gone; the priest did not cure, he examined and pronounced. Which is why the Gospels are so startling at this exact point. A leper came to Christ saying, If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean. And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him, and saith unto him, I will; be thou clean.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the hairy arch above the eye; in Scripture, named among all the hair the cleansed leper was to shave off on the seventh day.
webster_full: EYEBROW, n. The hairy arch above the eye.
LEPROSY, n. A foul cutaneous disease, appearing in dry, white, thin, scurfy scabs.
CLEANSING, n. The act of purifying or making clean; purification.
PRONOUNCE, v.t. To declare or affirm; as, the priest shall pronounce him clean.
HYSSOP, n. A plant used in the Mosaic rites of purification.
scriptures: Lev 14:9

But it shall be on the seventh day, that he shall shave all his hair off his head and his beard and his eyebrows, even all his hair he shall shave off: and he shall wash his clothes, also he shall wash his flesh in water, and he shall be clean.
Lev 14:2
This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing: He shall be brought unto the priest:
Lev 14:7
And he shall sprinkle upon him that is to be cleansed from the leprosy seven times, and shall pronounce him clean, and shall let the living bird loose into the open field.
Mar 1:41
And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him, and saith unto him, I will; be thou clean.
corruption_summary: Ceremonial law is read as arbitrary ritualism, when its thoroughness taught Israel the totality of defilement and of cleansing, and pointed to a Cleanser who touched what the law could only examine.
corruption_paragraphs: Leviticus 14 is often skimmed as primitive ceremony, and its structure repays a slower reading. Nothing in the rite makes a leper clean; every element of it presupposes that the plague of leprosy is healed in the leper. The priest went forth out of the camp to look, and if it was gone he began the cleansing. So the ritual is a picture of restoration to the congregation, not a cure, and its exhaustiveness — every hair, the eyebrows named — taught that defilement had reached all of a man and that the removal must reach all of him too.

The Gospel scenes stand directly against this background and every Jewish reader felt it. A leper approaches, which he should not; Christ puts out his hand and touches him, which under the law would defile the toucher; and the defilement runs the wrong way, for the man is cleansed instead of Christ being unclean. He then sends him to the priest to offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a testimony unto them — which means a priest somewhere in Israel had to open Leviticus 14 and perform a ritual he had perhaps never once used.

“the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing” — what the chapter is.

pos: n. (the sight of the eyes; in Psalm 18, God's own seeing)
etymology: From eye and sight. The Authorized Version uses it once, and not of a man's vision at all but of God's: the LORD recompensed David according to the cleanness of his hands in his eyesight.
biblical_def: Therefore hath the LORD recompensed me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his eyesight. The claim sounds presumptuous until the psalm is read whole. David is not asserting sinlessness; the psalm opens with a man in the floods of ungodly men, the sorrows of hell compassing him about, crying out of a distress he had no power to end — and the deliverance is entirely God's, described in the language of earthquake and storm: he bowed the heavens also, and came down. What David is claiming is that in the particular matter of Saul, where he was accused and hunted, his hands were clean, and God has now judged the case. Verse 21 makes the ground plain: I have kept the ways of the LORD, and have not wickedly departed from my God. The vindication of a falsely accused man is a real category in Scripture and not a claim of merit. And the word eyesight carries the weight, because the judgment is rendered in God's seeing and not in the court of public report. Hebrews says the same for every man: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the sight of the eye; view; observation; in Scripture, God's own seeing, in which David's cause was judged.
webster_full: EYESIGHT, n. The sight of the eye; view; observation.
RECOMPENSE, v.t. To compensate; to make return of an equivalent for anything given, done or suffered.
VINDICATE, v.t. To defend; to justify; to support or maintain as true or correct against denial.
OMNISCIENCE, n. The faculty of knowing all things; infinite knowledge.
INTEGRITY, n. The entire, unimpaired state of anything; particularly of the mind; moral soundness.
scriptures: Therefore hath the LORD recompensed me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his eyesight.
The LORD rewarded me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands hath he recompensed me.
Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
Heb 4:13
Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.
corruption_summary: Reputation is treated as the real verdict on a life, so that a man vindicated by God but condemned by report counts as condemned; the psalm renders judgment in God's eyesight and leaves the public record where it lies.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 18 is a vindication psalm, and vindication is one of the great neglected comforts of Scripture for anyone who has been falsely accused. David spent years under a charge he could not refute by argument, since the accuser had the throne and the army. The psalm's answer is not that he cleared his name but that God recompensed him according to the cleanness of his hands in his eyesight. The court that matters was never the one in session. Peter applies the same to Christ, who, when he suffered, threatened not, but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously.

The same eyesight is the terror of the hypocrite and the reason there is no such thing as a secret sin. Hebrews puts it without comfort: all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do. The two uses are one doctrine. A God who sees everything can be trusted to vindicate the wronged precisely because he can be relied on to expose the wrong, and a man who wants the first had better make his peace with the second.

pos: n. (a burning or feverish swelling; among the diseases of the curse and of the priest's examination)
etymology: From Latin inflammare, to set on fire. The Authorized Version uses it twice: of a burning in the skin the priest was to judge, and among the plagues threatened on a covenant-breaking nation.
biblical_def: The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish. The word stands in the great catalogue of the curses of Deuteronomy 28, and the shape of that chapter is what matters. Fourteen verses of blessing come first, and they are lavish: blessed shalt thou be in the city, and blessed shalt thou be in the field; blessed shall be thy basket and thy store; and all these blessings shall come on thee, and overtake thee, if thou shalt hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God. Then the hinge: but it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken, that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee. Fifty-four verses follow. The other use of the word is clinical and kind — a priest examining a burn on a man's skin and pronouncing him clean, for it is an inflammation of the burning. The same word covers a national judgment and a small mercy in a doctor's hands, and the law that wrote both is one law.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a redness, heat and swelling in any part of the body, attended with pain; in Scripture, both a skin condition the priest judged and a plague of the covenant curses.
webster_full: INFLAMMATION, n. A redness and swelling of any part of an animal body, attended with heat, pain, and febrile symptoms.
CONSUMPTION, n. A wasting of flesh; a gradual decay or diminution of the body.
BLASTING, n. A blast; destruction by a pernicious wind; in Scripture, a blight upon grain.
CURSE, n. Malediction; the expression of a wish of evil to another; in Scripture, the sentence of the law upon transgression.
COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act.
scriptures: The LORD shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew; and they shall pursue thee until thou perish.

And if the bright spot stay in his place, and spread not in the skin, but it be somewhat dark; it is a rising of the burning, and the priest shall pronounce him clean: for it is an inflammation of the burning.
Deu 28:2
And all these blessings shall come on thee, and overtake thee, if thou shalt hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God.

But it shall come to pass, if thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command thee this day; that all these curses shall come upon thee, and overtake thee:
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 28 is used as a formula to read any individual illness as a personal curse, or else dismissed altogether; it is a national covenant sanction on Israel, and Christ bore its curse for his people.
corruption_paragraphs: Two misuses of this chapter are common and both are serious. The first turns it into a diagnostic tool: a man is sick, therefore a man is under curse, therefore find the sin. Job's friends worked that way and God rebuked them, and the Lord refused the same reasoning about the man born blind. Deuteronomy 28 is addressed to a nation under a particular covenant with particular sanctions, and the New Testament applies it to Israel's history rather than handing it to individuals as a ledger. The second misuse is to drop the chapter entirely, as though God does not deal with peoples in history, which Scripture asserts from Genesis to Revelation.

The resolution is in Galatians and it is the heart of the gospel: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. The curses of Deuteronomy 28 fell, in full, on One who had broken nothing. That is why a believer's illness is not a sanction but a chastening, dealt out by a Father to sons, and why Hebrews can say that whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth — a different word, a different purpose, and a different end.
roots_summary: Hebrew dalleqeth (H1816), a burning fever or inflammation; tsarebeth (H6867), a scar or inflammation of a burn; qelalah (H7045), a curse.
roots_lines: Hebrew dalleqeth (H1816) — an inflammation, a burning fever; Deuteronomy 28:22.
Hebrew tsarebeth (H6867) — the scar or inflammation of a burn; Leviticus 13:28.
Hebrew shachepheth (H7829) — a wasting, a consumption; first in the list of plagues.
Hebrew qelalah (H7045) — a curse, a vilification; all these curses shall come upon thee.
Hebrew shama' (H8085) — to hear, to hearken, to obey; if thou shalt hearken unto the voice of the LORD.

“it is an inflammation of the burning” — the priest pronouncing a man clean.
“all these blessings shall come on thee, and overtake thee” — the half that comes first.

pos: n. (a hindrance; in Mark 7, a defect of speech)
etymology: From Latin impedimentum, a hindrance, from in and pes, the foot — something that entangles the feet. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the man brought to Christ who was deaf and had an impediment in his speech.
biblical_def: And they bring unto him one that was deaf, and had an impediment in his speech; and they beseech him to put his hand upon him. What follows is one of the most physical healings in the Gospels. He took him aside from the multitude, put his fingers into his ears, spit and touched his tongue, looked up to heaven, sighed, and said, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened. Every gesture is fitted to a man who could not hear a word of instruction: the Lord speaks to him in the only language he has. The sigh is the detail that has always arrested readers — the Creator standing in a broken creation and grieving at what sin has done to a pair of ears. And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain. The crowd's verdict is the finest sentence in the chapter: He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak. Isaiah had written the programme centuries before: then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): that which hinders progress or motion; hindrance; obstruction; in Scripture, the defect of speech in the deaf man of Decapolis.
webster_full: IMPEDIMENT, n. That which hinders progress or motion; hindrance; obstruction; obstacle.
IMPEDIMENT, n. A defect which prevents clear utterance; as an impediment in speech.
DEAF, a. Not perceiving sounds; not receiving impressions from sonorous bodies through the air.
DUMB, a. Mute; silent; not speaking; incapable of speech.
COMPASSION, n. A suffering with another; painful sympathy; pity for the distressed.
scriptures: Mar 7:32
And they bring unto him one that was deaf, and had an impediment in his speech; and they beseech him to put his hand upon him.
Mar 7:34
And looking up to heaven, he sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened.
Mar 7:37
And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak.
Isa 35:6
Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert.
corruption_summary: The miracles are reduced to parables of inner awakening, or the sigh of Christ is emptied of real grief; Mark records a physical healing of a physical man, and a Saviour who groaned over the damage.
corruption_paragraphs: The demythologising reading takes this account as a symbol of spiritual deafness opened by encounter, and in doing so it loses the only thing that makes the symbol worth anything. A real man's ears were really opened, and he spake plain, and the people were beyond measure astonished. The symbolic meaning is genuine and secondary; it depends entirely on the event. Where the event evaporates, the symbol has nothing left to stand on and the Saviour it points to cannot open anything.

The sigh deserves its own line. Jesus looked up to heaven and sighed, and the same verb is used of the whole creation groaning in Romans 8 and of believers groaning within ourselves waiting for the redemption of our body. Christ is not detached from the ruin he is repairing; he grieves at it, weeps at a grave he is about to open, and is moved with compassion before he heals. The dictionary therefore refuses both the impassive deity of the philosophers and the modern therapeutic Jesus who only affirms. He groaned, and then he commanded, and the ears obeyed.
roots_summary: Greek mogilalos (G3424), speaking with difficulty; kophos (G2974), deaf or dumb; dianoigo (G1272), to open thoroughly.
roots_lines: Greek mogilalos (G3424) — speaking with difficulty, having an impediment; the one occurrence, Mark 7:32.
Greek kophos (G2974) — blunted, and so deaf or dumb; one that was deaf.
Greek dianoigo (G1272) — to open up completely; his ears were opened.
Greek stenazo (G4727) — to sigh, to groan; he sighed.
Aramaic ephphatha (G2188) — be opened; the word the Lord spoke.

“Ephphatha, that is, Be opened” — the word spoken over him.
“He hath done all things well” — the crowd's verdict.

pos: n. (one lame or disabled in the limbs; the man healed at Lystra)
etymology: Old English crypel, from the root of creep. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the man at Lystra, impotent in his feet, a cripple from his mother's womb, who never had walked.
biblical_def: And there sat a certain man at Lystra, impotent in his feet, being a cripple from his mother's womb, who never had walked. Luke stacks the clauses so that no one can mistake the case for a temporary weakness. The same man heard Paul speak, and Paul, stedfastly beholding him, and perceiving that he had faith to be healed, said with a loud voice, Stand upright on thy feet. And he leaped and walked. The crowd's reaction is the reason this account is in the book: they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men, and they called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercurius, and the priest of Jupiter brought oxen and garlands to the gates. The apostles rent their clothes and ran in among the people crying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein. Shortly after, the same crowd stoned Paul and drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a lame person; primarily, one who creeps, halts or limps; one who has lost or never enjoyed the use of a limb.
webster_full: CRIPPLE, n. A lame person; primarily, one who creeps, halts or limps.
IMPOTENT, a. Weak; feeble; wanting strength or power; unable by feebleness to perform anything.
LAME, a. Crippled or disabled in a limb; hobbling; not able to walk without halting.
IDOLATRY, n. The worship of idols, images, or anything made by hands, or which is not God.
VANITY, n. Empty pleasure; vain pursuit; idle show; in Scripture, an idol, a thing of nought.
scriptures: Act 14:8
And there sat a certain man at Lystra, impotent in his feet, being a cripple from his mother's womb, who never had walked:
Said with a loud voice, Stand upright on thy feet. And he leaped and walked.
And when the people saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in the speech of Lycaonia, The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men.

And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:
corruption_summary: Honour given to a servant of God is accepted rather than refused, and the miracle worker becomes the centre of the meeting; Paul and Barnabas tore their clothes and ran into the crowd to stop it.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 14 is the plainest apostolic refusal of personality cult in the New Testament, and the violence of the refusal is the point. They rent their clothes and ran in among the people. Not a modest disclaimer from the platform — a public horror. We also are men of like passions with you. The same reflex appears whenever the question arises: Peter lifting Cornelius off the floor with Stand up; I myself also am a man; the angel in Revelation telling John, See thou do it not: worship God. Every one of them treats misdirected honour as an emergency.

The sermon Paul preaches to a pagan crowd is worth noticing for its starting point, since he had no Old Testament to appeal to. He begins at creation — the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein — and moves to providence, that God left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness. And these sayings scarce restrained the people. The idolatry of the crowd was so strong that even a direct refusal barely held it, which is a sober note for anyone with a following.

Greek homoiopathes (G3663) — of like feelings or nature; men of like passions with you.

pos: adj. (having a crooked or curved back; hunchbacked)
etymology: From crook, to bend, and back, with the old participial ending. The Authorized Version uses it once, first in the list of blemishes that barred a son of Aaron from the altar.
biblical_def: Or crookbackt, or a dwarf, or that hath a blemish in his eye. The word heads the last group of blemishes in Leviticus 21, and the same two verses govern it as govern the rest: the man eats the bread of his God, of the most holy and of the holy, and only he shall not go in unto the vail, nor come nigh unto the altar, because he hath a blemish. The bar is to the altar, not to the priesthood, and the reason given is the protection of the type. Luke gives the Gospel counterpart in a sabbath synagogue: there was a woman which had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years, and was bowed together, and could in no wise lift up herself. Christ called her to him and said, Woman, thou art loosed from thine infirmity, and laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and glorified God — and he called her a daughter of Abraham whom Satan hath bound. The ruler of the synagogue objected about the day. Paul's own thorn supplies the last word for every believer whose body is not made straight in this life: My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): having a crooked back; hunched; in Scripture, first among the blemishes barring a priest from the altar.
webster_full: CROOKBACKED, a. Having a crooked back.
CROOK, v.t. To bend; to turn from a straight line; to make a hook or curve.
INFIRMITY, n. An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; feebleness.
DEFORMITY, n. Any unnatural state of the shape or form; want of that uniformity which constitutes beauty.
SUFFICIENT, a. Enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants.
scriptures: Only he shall not go in unto the vail, nor come nigh unto the altar, because he hath a blemish; that he profane not my sanctuaries: for I the LORD do sanctify them.
He shall eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy, and of the holy.
And, behold, there was a woman which had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years, and was bowed together, and could in no wise lift up herself.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
corruption_summary: Weakness is treated as a problem to be solved before a person can be useful, when Scripture makes the unhealed thorn the very place God displays his strength, and calls the bowed woman a daughter of Abraham.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul asked three times for the thorn to be removed and it was not, and the answer he received has carried more afflicted Christians than any healing in the book: My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. His conclusion is not resignation but a reversal — most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. A theology that can only account for God's goodness in the removal of weakness has no category for the apostle who wrote most of the New Testament, and it abandons every believer whose body stays bent.

Luke 13 guards the other side, so that the sufficiency of grace is never used to argue that God is indifferent to bodies. Christ saw the woman, called her, laid hands on her, and made her straight, and he named the bondage for what it was: Satan hath bound her, lo, these eighteen years. Both things are true and the church needs both. God heals, and God sustains those he does not heal, and the resurrection of the body is the promise that settles the account for everyone in either group.
roots_summary: Hebrew gibben (H1384), crookbacked, hunched; muwm (H3971), a blemish; Greek astheneia (G769), weakness or infirmity.
roots_lines: Hebrew gibben (H1384) — crookbacked, hunched; the one occurrence, Leviticus 21:20.
Hebrew muwm (H3971) — a blemish, a defect; because he hath a blemish.
Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to pollute; that he profane not my sanctuaries.
Greek astheneia (G769) — feebleness, infirmity; a spirit of infirmity eighteen years.
Greek anorthoo (G461) — to set straight again; she was made straight.

“was bowed together, and could in no wise lift up herself” — the woman Christ loosed.
“My grace is sufficient for thee” — the answer to the thorn that stayed.
